headline.en: Tessellation is fitting shapes together with no gaps—only certain shapes can tile a plane perfectly

universal_truth.en: Fitting together is a design problem; the right pieces interlock, the wrong pieces leave gaps

fun_facts.en: Only three regular polygons can tessellate on their own: triangles, squares, and hexagons
Bees build hexagonal honeycomb cells—the most efficient shape for storing honey with minimal wax
M.C. Escher became famous for tessellations using interlocking fish, birds, and fantastical creatures

discussion_questions.en: Why can some shapes tile while others can't?
What in life needs to 'fit together' with no gaps?
Where do you see tessellation in the built environment?

script.en: Look at a tile floor or honeycomb: shapes fitting together with no gaps, no overlaps. This is tessellation—and only certain shapes can do it. Nature discovered this for beehives; mathematicians proved which shapes work and why.

text.en: I want to learn something new

response.en: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

script.en: You can tile a floor with squares, but not with regular pentagons. Some shapes fit together perfectly; others always leave gaps. What determines whether a shape can tessellate?

prompt.en: What determines if a shape can tessellate?

text.en: The angles at each corner must add up to exactly 360 degrees—only certain shapes have angles that make this possible

response.en: Yes. Where corners meet, angles must sum to 360°. Squares have 90° angles—four meet perfectly. Hexagons have 120°—three meet perfectly. Pentagons have 108°—they can't combine to 360°.

text.en: Simple shapes with straight edges can tessellate

response.en: Straight edges help, but the key is angle mathematics...

script.en: At every meeting point, angles must total exactly 360 degrees—a full rotation. Squares: 4 × 90° = 360°. Triangles: 6 × 60° = 360°. Hexagons: 3 × 120° = 360°. Pentagons: 108° × 3 = 324°. Doesn't work.

script.en: Bees build hexagonal cells because hexagons are the most efficient tessellating shape—enclosing the most area with the least perimeter. Minimum wax, maximum honey storage. Evolution solved the same problem mathematicians later proved optimal.

script.en: You can combine different shapes that tessellate together—octagons with squares, for instance. Escher took this further, warping shapes into creatures that still interlock perfectly. The constraints of tessellation sparked wild creativity.

title.en: Fit Check - What Interlocks in Your Life?

activity.en: Consider the elements of your life—work, relationships, hobbies, rest. Do they tessellate (fit together smoothly) or leave gaps and overlaps? What adjustments would help everything interlock better? Good design means pieces that fit.
